title: Ask Every Dying Cell Two Questions

scenes.tts: How do you tell how a cell died? Looking is not enough. A dying cell's appearance names where it ended up, not what killed it. So we ask each cell two questions. One is about a lipid. The other is about the membrane.

scenes.visual: A cell with a question mark; appearance leads to an endpoint but a crossed-out link to the cause; two question chips aim at the cell.
scenes.narration: How do you tell how a cell died? Looking is not enough. A dying cell's appearance names where it ended up, not what killed it. So we ask each cell two questions. One is about a lipid. The other is about the membrane.

scenes.tts: A healthy cell keeps a lipid called phosphatidylserine on the inner face of its plasma membrane. Annexin five is a protein that binds this lipid, with calcium. From outside, it cannot reach the lipid. Propidium iodide is a D N A dye. Live cells keep it out.
scenes.caption: A healthy cell keeps a lipid called phosphatidylserine on the inner face of its plasma membrane. Annexin V is a protein that binds this lipid, with calcium. From outside, it cannot reach the lipid. Propidium iodide is a DNA dye. Live cells keep it out.
scenes.visual: Membrane as two bars; lipid heads on the inner bar; annexin V and PI approach from outside and bounce off; both readouts show minus.
scenes.narration: A healthy cell keeps a lipid called phosphatidylserine on the inner face of its plasma membrane. Annexin V is a protein that binds this lipid, with calcium. From outside, it cannot reach the lipid. Propidium iodide is a DNA dye. Live cells keep it out.

scenes.tts: Now the cell dies by apoptosis. The lipid turns up on the outer face. Annexin five can reach it and bind. That binding means the lipid is reachable from outside. But the membrane still holds, so propidium iodide stays out. This cell is annexin five positive and P I negative. It is the clearest apoptotic signal.
scenes.caption: Now the cell dies by apoptosis. The lipid turns up on the outer face. Annexin V can reach it and bind. That binding means the lipid is reachable from outside. But the membrane still holds, so propidium iodide stays out. This cell is annexin V positive and PI negative. It is the clearest apoptotic signal.
scenes.visual: Lipid heads move to the outer face; annexin V blobs bind; PI dots bounce off; annexin V readout turns positive.
scenes.narration: Now the cell dies by apoptosis. The lipid turns up on the outer face. Annexin V can reach it and bind. That binding means the lipid is reachable from outside. But the membrane still holds, so propidium iodide stays out. This cell is annexin V positive and PI negative. It is the clearest apoptotic signal.

scenes.tts: Then comes a leak. In culture, with nothing to eat it, an apoptotic cell generally becomes leaky. This is called secondary necrosis. Propidium iodide enters and stains the D N A. Its entry means the membrane is leaky, whatever made it so. Now the cell is positive for both.
scenes.caption: Then comes a leak. In culture, with nothing to eat it, an apoptotic cell generally becomes leaky. This is called secondary necrosis. Propidium iodide enters and stains the DNA. Its entry means the membrane is leaky, whatever made it so. Now the cell is positive for both.
scenes.visual: Gaps open in the membrane bars; PI dots pass through and the DNA blob turns orange; PI readout turns positive.
scenes.narration: Then comes a leak. In culture, with nothing to eat it, an apoptotic cell generally becomes leaky. This is called secondary necrosis. Propidium iodide enters and stains the DNA. Its entry means the membrane is leaky, whatever made it so. Now the cell is positive for both.

scenes.tts: Now read the plot. In this made up data set, a flow cytometer reads ten thousand Jurkat cells after six hours of drug. Each cell lands in one of four boxes. Five thousand eight hundred are negative for both. Two thousand nine hundred are annexin five positive only. One thousand are positive for both. Three hundred are positive for propidium iodide only. A double positive cell is a puzzle. It could be a late apoptotic cell, or a cell that died by necrosis from the start. One time point cannot tell them apart.
scenes.caption: Now read the plot. In this made-up data set, a flow cytometer reads 10,000 Jurkat cells after 6 hours of drug. Each cell lands in one of four boxes. 5,800 are negative for both. 2,900 are annexin V positive only. 1,000 are positive for both. 300 are positive for propidium iodide only. A double-positive cell is a puzzle. It could be a late apoptotic cell, or a cell that died by necrosis from the start. One time point cannot tell them apart.
scenes.visual: Four-quadrant plot fills with the lesson's counts; two cells of different origin land in the double-positive box.

scenes.tts: So follow the cells in time. An apoptotic cell exposes the lipid first, and stays P I negative for a while. It should pass through the annexin five positive box before it turns double positive. A time course can tell the two deaths apart. Keep the rule. One marker reports one event. Combine markers, and follow them in time.
